title: TOEFL iBT Reading Practice Test 22
instructions: Read each passage carefully and answer all questions. You have 35 minutes. Questions test factual understanding, vocabulary, inference, and the ability to identify main ideas.

passages.title: Earthquake Early Warning Systems
passages.text:
An earthquake early warning system is a rapid detection and alerting network designed to notify the public and critical infrastructure of strong ground motion seconds to minutes before shaking arrives at a specific location. Unlike earthquake prediction, which attempts to forecast when and where earthquakes will occur, early warning systems operate by detecting earthquakes that have already begun, measuring their magnitude and location in real time, and disseminating warnings to areas likely to experience strong shaking. The most advanced systems can issue alerts within 3 to 10 seconds of earthquake detection, providing crucial time for protective actions such as securing heavy objects, stopping elevators, or triggering automatic safety systems in hospitals and power plants.

The technical foundation of early warning relies on a dense network of seismometers and accelerometers positioned throughout seismically active regions. When an earthquake ruptures, P-waves (primary waves) travel faster than S-waves (secondary waves) and the destructive ground motion that follows. By detecting P-waves and rapidly calculating the earthquake's magnitude and depth, algorithms can estimate the intensity of S-waves expected at each location. Japan pioneered this technology in the 1990s and continues to operate the most comprehensive system, with over 1,000 sensors across the country. Mexico, Romania, and the United States have since developed similar capabilities, particularly in California and the Pacific Northwest.

The effectiveness of earthquake early warning depends critically on the accuracy of rapid magnitude estimation and the speed of alert dissemination. Modern systems use seismic moment magnitudes and Ground Motion Prediction Equations (GMPEs) to forecast peak ground acceleration and velocity at distant sites. However, very large earthquakes sometimes produce lower-than-expected initial motion estimates because the rupture evolves over longer durations than standard algorithms anticipate. This phenomenon, known as the "blind zone," describes areas very close to the epicentre where shaking arrives before any warning can be issued, a fundamental limitation that cannot be overcome by faster technology alone.

Studies evaluating early warning performance in Japan and Mexico demonstrate that systems can significantly reduce injuries and fatalities when appropriate protective actions are taken. After the 2011 Tōhoku earthquake in Japan, the warning system reduced casualty rates by alerting residents seconds before strong shaking arrived in Tokyo, over 200 kilometres away. In Mexico City, the system provides approximately 60 seconds of warning for earthquakes originating on the Pacific coast, enough time for people to evacuate buildings and seek shelter under sturdy objects. However, the effectiveness depends entirely on public awareness, rapid dissemination through multiple channels (broadcast, mobile networks, sirens), and rapid human response.

Despite their proven value, early warning systems face persistent challenges. Earthquake variability means that ground motion predictions carry significant uncertainty, occasionally leading to false alarms or missed predictions. Aging sensor networks require continuous maintenance and capital investment. In lower-income countries with high seismic risk, such as Nepal and Indonesia, the lack of funding and technical expertise has limited system deployment. Additionally, public awareness and education campaigns must be sustained continuously, as memory of earthquake risks fades in periods without major seismic activity. The future of early warning technology lies in integrating traditional seismic sensors with GPS networks, seafloor pressure sensors for submarine earthquakes, and artificial intelligence algorithms that improve magnitude estimation in real time.

passages.title: Human Gut Microbiome
passages.text:
The human gut microbiome comprises approximately 30 to 40 trillion microbial cells distributed throughout the digestive tract, representing species diversity greater than the number of cells in the human body itself. The vast majority of these organisms are bacteria, with smaller populations of archaea, viruses (bacteriophages), and fungi. Contrary to older medical paradigms that treated bacteria as purely pathogenic invaders, modern research has revealed that the gut microbiome performs essential functions including nutrient metabolism, immune system development, synthesis of vitamins (particularly B vitamins and vitamin K), and production of neurotransmitters that influence mood and cognitive function.

The composition of the gut microbiome is established early in infancy through colonization by maternal bacteria during vaginal delivery or supplementary microbes from the birth environment. By 18 months of age, the microbial community stabilizes into a relatively stable configuration that persists throughout adulthood, though the relative abundance of different species fluctuates in response to dietary changes, antibiotic use, and disease states. The two dominant bacterial phyla are Firmicutes and Bacteroidetes, which together constitute approximately 90 percent of the total bacterial population. Within these phyla, genera such as Bacteroides, Faecalibacterium, Roseburia, and Prevotella occupy distinct metabolic niches, fermenting different dietary carbohydrates and producing short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) such as butyrate and propionate.

Short-chain fatty acids produced by microbial fermentation of dietary fibre represent one of the most important functional outputs of the healthy microbiome. These molecules are absorbed by the intestinal epithelium and enter systemic circulation, where they regulate glucose metabolism, reduce inflammation, and strengthen the intestinal barrier by promoting tight junction integrity. Butyrate specifically serves as the preferred energy source for colonocytes and plays crucial roles in histone deacetylase inhibition, a mechanism relevant to cancer prevention. Epidemiological studies demonstrate that populations consuming high-fibre diets harbour microbiomes rich in butyrate-producing bacteria and exhibit lower rates of colorectal cancer, metabolic syndrome, and inflammatory bowel disease.

Disruption of normal microbiome composition, termed dysbiosis, is associated with multiple disease states including obesity, type 2 diabetes, inflammatory bowel disease, Crohn's disease, and potentially neurological conditions such as autism spectrum disorder and Parkinson's disease. Dysbiosis is typically characterized by reduced microbial diversity, proliferation of pathogenic taxa such as Clostridium difficile, and depletion of beneficial taxa. The mechanisms linking dysbiosis to disease remain incompletely understood but likely involve impaired production of metabolites like butyrate, increased intestinal permeability, and dysregulated immune responses. Antibiotic use, high-fat and high-sugar diets, and stress have all been documented as dysbiosis-inducing factors.

Therapeutic strategies targeting the microbiome have emerged as promising interventions for microbiome-associated diseases. Faecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) is a well-established treatment for recurrent Clostridium difficile infections, with cure rates exceeding 90 percent in clinical trials. Probiotic supplementation with specific live bacterial strains has shown modest benefits in certain conditions but lacks the broad efficacy of FMT. Dietary interventions promoting increased fibre consumption, particularly from whole grains, legumes, and vegetables, remain the most evidence-based approach for improving microbiome composition and associated health outcomes. Emerging research on bacteriophage therapies and targeted antimicrobials designed to eliminate pathogenic species while preserving beneficial bacteria represents a frontier in personalized microbiome medicine.

questions.prompt: According to paragraph 1, how quickly can the most advanced earthquake early warning systems issue alerts?
questions.correctAnswer: Within 3 to 10 seconds of earthquake detection
questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 states: 'The most advanced systems can issue alerts within 3 to 10 seconds of earthquake detection.'
options: Within 3 to 10 seconds of earthquake detection

questions.prompt: The word 'dense' in paragraph 2 is closest in meaning to:
questions.explanation: In the phrase 'dense network of seismometers,' dense refers to a thick, closely packed distribution across a region.

questions.prompt: According to paragraph 2, which country pioneered earthquake early warning technology in the 1990s?
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 states: 'Japan pioneered this technology in the 1990s and continues to operate the most comprehensive system.'

questions.prompt: What can be inferred from paragraph 3 about the 'blind zone' phenomenon?
questions.correctAnswer: It represents an unavoidable technological limitation in earthquake early warning
questions.explanation: The passage states it is 'a fundamental limitation that cannot be overcome by faster technology alone,' implying inherent physical constraints.
options: It can be eliminated with more seismic sensors
It represents an unavoidable technological limitation in earthquake early warning
It makes early warning systems completely ineffective

questions.prompt: Why does the author mention Mexico City in paragraph 4?
questions.correctAnswer: To provide a specific example of early warning time and its practical application
questions.explanation: The example demonstrates that the system provides 60 seconds of warning, enough time for protective actions, illustrating the system's real-world effectiveness.
options: To argue that Mexico has a better system than Japan
To provide a specific example of early warning time and its practical application
To suggest that early warning systems are less effective in developing countries
To explain why the 2011 Tōhoku earthquake was so destructive

questions.prompt: According to paragraph 5, which of the following is NOT mentioned as a challenge facing early warning systems?
questions.explanation: The passage mentions earthquake variability, aging sensors, funding limitations, public awareness, and suggests future integration of technologies—but does not mention international cooperation as a challenge.
options: Earthquake variability leading to prediction uncertainty

questions.prompt: According to paragraph 4, what distance away from the epicentre did the 2011 Tōhoku earthquake system provide warnings to Tokyo?
questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 states: 'the warning system reduced casualty rates by alerting residents seconds before strong shaking arrived in Tokyo, over 200 kilometres away.'

questions.prompt: The word 'dissemination' in paragraph 4 is closest in meaning to:
questions.explanation: Dissemination refers to the process of spreading information quickly and widely through multiple channels.

questions.prompt: Which best expresses the essential information in this sentence: 'By detecting P-waves and rapidly calculating the earthquake's magnitude and depth, algorithms can estimate the intensity of S-waves expected at each location.'
questions.correctAnswer: Algorithms use fast P-wave data to predict the strength of damaging S-waves
questions.explanation: The sentence explains how systems detect fast-moving waves to forecast the intensity of slower, destructive waves at different locations.
options: Seismometers can only detect P-waves, not S-waves
Algorithms use fast P-wave data to predict the strength of damaging S-waves
S-waves always arrive before P-waves are detected
Earthquakes release only P-waves in the early stage

questions.prompt: Complete a summary of the passage. Select THREE answer choices that express the most important ideas.
questions.explanation: A describes the core technology and advantage, C addresses real-world effectiveness and limitations, E identifies remaining challenges and future directions.
options: A. Earthquake early warning systems detect ongoing earthquakes and issue alerts within seconds, providing time for protective actions.
B. Japan is the only country with an earthquake early warning system.
C. These systems are most effective when supported by rapid dissemination technology and public awareness, but fundamental physical limitations restrict their reach.
D. Faecal microbiota transplantation is more effective than early warning systems.
E. Persistent challenges include earthquake variability, aging infrastructure, funding limitations in developing countries, and the need for sustained public education.
F. Earthquake prediction is now more accurate than early warning detection.

questions.prompt: According to paragraph 1, how many microbial cells does the human gut microbiome comprise?
questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 states: 'The human gut microbiome comprises approximately 30 to 40 trillion microbial cells.'

questions.prompt: The word 'paradigm' in paragraph 1 is closest in meaning to:
questions.correctAnswer: established framework or model of thinking
questions.explanation: A paradigm refers to a conceptual model or conventional way of understanding something within a field.
options: established framework or model of thinking

questions.prompt: According to paragraph 2, what percentage of bacterial population do Firmicutes and Bacteroidetes together represent?
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 states: 'The two dominant bacterial phyla are Firmicutes and Bacteroidetes, which together constitute approximately 90 percent of the total bacterial population.'

questions.prompt: What can be inferred from paragraph 3 about the relationship between dietary fiber and colorectal cancer risk?
questions.correctAnswer: Higher fiber intake is associated with lower colorectal cancer rates
questions.explanation: The passage states that high-fiber diet consumers 'exhibit lower rates of colorectal cancer,' indicating a protective relationship.
options: Dietary fiber has no effect on cancer risk
High-fiber diets increase colorectal cancer risk
Higher fiber intake is associated with lower colorectal cancer rates
Colorectal cancer is caused exclusively by dysbiosis

questions.prompt: Why does the author discuss butyrate specifically in paragraph 3?
questions.correctAnswer: To illustrate a key mechanism by which the microbiome promotes health
questions.explanation: Butyrate is presented as an example of an SCFA with multiple important functions (energy source, cancer prevention, inflammation reduction), demonstrating microbiome health benefits.
options: To argue that butyrate is harmful to intestinal health
To illustrate a key mechanism by which the microbiome promotes health
To suggest that all SCFAs are equally important

questions.prompt: According to paragraph 4, which of the following is NOT mentioned as a disease associated with dysbiosis?
questions.explanation: The passage lists obesity, type 2 diabetes, inflammatory bowel disease, Crohn's disease, and possibly autism and Parkinson's—but does not mention hypertension.

questions.prompt: According to paragraph 5, what is the cure rate for faecal microbiota transplantation in treating recurrent Clostridium difficile infections?
questions.explanation: Paragraph 5 states: 'Faecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) is a well-established treatment for recurrent Clostridium difficile infections, with cure rates exceeding 90 percent.'

questions.prompt: The word 'dysbiosis' in paragraph 4 is closest in meaning to:
questions.explanation: Dysbiosis is defined in the passage as 'disruption of normal microbiome composition,' characterized by reduced diversity and pathogenic changes.

questions.prompt: Which best expresses the essential information in this sentence: 'Dietary interventions promoting increased fibre consumption, particularly from whole grains, legumes, and vegetables, remain the most evidence-based approach for improving microbiome composition and associated health outcomes.'
questions.correctAnswer: Eating more fiber-rich foods is the most scientifically supported way to improve microbiome health
questions.explanation: The sentence identifies dietary fiber increase as the most evidence-backed strategy for restoring healthy microbiome composition.
options: Supplements are better than whole foods for microbiome health
Eating more fiber-rich foods is the most scientifically supported way to improve microbiome health
Fiber consumption has no effect on the microbiome
Legumes are harmful to microbiome composition

questions.prompt: Select THREE answer choices that express the most important ideas in the passage.
questions.explanation: B describes the composition and scale of the microbiome, D explains key functional roles, F outlines emerging therapeutic strategies.
options: A. All bacteria in the human gut are pathogenic and cause disease.
B. The gut microbiome comprises trillions of microbes that perform essential functions including nutrient metabolism and immune system development.
C. Firmicutes are more important than any other bacterial phylum.
D. Short-chain fatty acids produced by the microbiome regulate metabolism and prevent inflammation through multiple mechanisms.
E. Dysbiosis can only be caused by antibiotic use.
F. Therapeutic approaches range from faecal microbiota transplantation to dietary fiber interventions, with fiber-based approaches being the most evidence-supported long-term strategy.
